name: From the Blues to Hip-Hop: The Sound of Black America
description: Blues, jazz, rock and roll, soul and rap: the music made by Black Americans that changed pop for everyone, from Bessie Smith's records to Beyoncé's stage shows.

checkpoints.name: Roots
checkpoints.note: The blues grows from songs of work and sorrow in the American South, and jazz forms around the same time in New Orleans. Bessie Smith makes the blues a record-selling art, Louis Armstrong turns jazz into a soloist's music, and Duke Ellington builds an orchestra in New York during the Harlem Renaissance. George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue (1924) carries jazz sounds into the concert hall.

checkpoints.name: Protest and rhythm
checkpoints.note: Strange Fruit, a song protesting lynching, is recorded by Billie Holiday in 1939 and stays a landmark of protest music. Jazz moves from dance halls to small clubs, and electric guitars and driving beats shape rhythm and blues, the sound that young players such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Ray Charles will carry forward.

checkpoints.name: Rock, soul and new jazz
checkpoints.note: Rock and roll arrives in the 1950s with Chuck Berry and Little Richard, while Ray Charles joins gospel and blues. Miles Davis's Kind of Blue (1959) and John Coltrane's A Love Supreme (1965) transform jazz. Berry Gordy founds Motown in Detroit in 1959, and The Supremes, Aretha Franklin, Nina Simone and Jimi Hendrix follow.

checkpoints.name: Message and block party
checkpoints.note: Marvin Gaye's What's Going On (1971) and the albums of Stevie Wonder show soul speaking about the wider world. Hip-hop begins at parties in the Bronx in 1973, and Rapper's Delight (1979) takes it to the radio. Michael Jackson's Thriller (1982) becomes one of the biggest-selling albums ever.

checkpoints.name: Hip-hop takes over
checkpoints.note: N.W.A and the Wu-Tang Clan make rap a major force, and Nas's Illmatic (1994) is widely admired for its detail. Lauryn Hill's The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill (1998) blends rap and soul, while Prince, Whitney Houston and Beyoncé keep Black American styles at the centre of pop.
